**Reading map:** Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, *Mathematics for Machine Learning* (2020), §2.4. This is an original lesson using our delivery-operations example—not reproduced textbook content.

## Why the concept matters

Each delivery feature vector is an element of R^2. The set of all possible real-valued feature vectors is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication; this is what makes linear transformations meaningful.

## Define the mathematical relationship

$$
\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol z\in V,\ a,b\in\mathbb R\Longrightarrow a\boldsymbol x+b\boldsymbol z\in V
$$

The displayed relationship is the main object to analyse. Specify the relevant dimensions, quantities and assumptions before using it. It should be read as a mathematical statement, not merely a programming shorthand.

## Work through an original example

For x=(1,1)^T and z=(2,2)^T, the combination 2x-z=(0,0)^T remains in R^2. By contrast, the set of physical delivery distances restricted to nonnegative values is not closed under subtraction, so it is not itself a vector space.

## What follows, and what does not

Separating physical constraints from mathematical vector-space structure prevents false claims. The model may operate in R^2 while the valid real-world inputs occupy only a subset.

## Test your reasoning

Is the set {(x,y):x+y=1} a vector subspace of R^2? Test whether it contains the zero vector.
